passage:
Chetan: Disha! Big finding. Stores that play music sell 20% more. Let's put speakers in all 60 branches 🎉
Disha: nice spot! before we buy speakers, can I poke at it a bit?
Chetan: poke away
Disha: which stores play music right now?
Chetan: mostly the mall ones i think
Disha: mall stores also get far more footfall. that alone could explain both things
Disha: and maybe busy stores switch music on because they're busy, not the other way round
Chetan: hmm 😅
Disha: it could even be coincidence, it's just one quarter of data
Chetan: ok so what do you suggest
Disha: pick 10 similar high-street stores. music in 5, none in the other 5, same 6 weeks. then compare
Chetan: fair. i'll pitch it as a pilot on Monday
Disha: 👍 and if music still wins, we'll know it's the music

qa.q: How much more did stores with music sell, according to Chetan?
qa.a: 20% more.

qa.q: What does Disha's request to "poke at it" suggest about Disha's attitude?
qa.a: Disha feels curious and careful rather than swept up in the excitement, wanting to test the link before trusting it.

qa.q: What test does Disha propose, and why is it strong?
qa.a: Music in five similar high-street stores and none in five others for the same six weeks, because the comparison separates the music from footfall and luck.

qa.q: How does Chetan react to Disha's questions?
qa.a: Chetan is a little sheepish at first but finds the pilot fair and agrees to pitch it.

grounding: Shows an analyst asking whether a third cause, reverse direction or coincidence explains a link, and proposing a comparison group before claiming cause.

subtype: After this, therefore because of this [Actor]
passage: In the dry last week of May in their village near Latur, the fields were cracked and even the goats looked tired. Ramesh climbed onto the flat roof, tied a red cloth round his head and did a stomping rain dance while his cousin Pooja giggled below. The next afternoon, black clouds rolled in and the first rain hammered the tin roofs. Ramesh ran out, soaking. "I did it! My dance brought the rain!" "Ramesh, it rains every June," Pooja said. "Aaji said last week the clouds were coming." "But it came after my dance," Ramesh said firmly, water dripping from his nose. That evening he began planning a special dance for Sunday's cricket match.

qa.q: What did Ramesh tie round his head for the dance?
qa.a: A red cloth.

qa.q: Why is Ramesh so sure his dance brought the rain?
qa.a: The rain came right after his dance, so he feels proud and powerful, as if whatever came next must have been caused by him 😄

qa.q: How could Pooja or Aaji help Ramesh test his idea?
qa.a: They could remind him that the rains come every June and ask him to notice whether it also rains on days when he doesn't dance.

qa.q: How does Pooja see the rain?
qa.a: Pooja sees it as the usual June rain that Aaji had already said was coming, not as the result of the dance.

grounding: Shows a child believing his dance brought the rain because the rain came right after it.

passage: After Durga Puja, Arnab came back to school with a red-and-gold thread tied on his wrist from the pandal near his house in Kolkata. The week before the holidays he had scored a miserable 11 out of 30 in the physics unit test, much lower than usual. On Friday's retest he scored 22. "It's the thread," he announced at the tiffin table, holding up his wrist like a trophy. "Pandal power." Zubin chewed his luchi. "Weren't you down with a fever during the first test?" "So?" "And the whole class scored higher this time. Sir said it was an easier paper." Arnab frowned, then retied the thread tighter. "The thread helped anyway. I'm never taking it off."

qa.q: What did Arnab score in Friday's retest?
qa.a: He scored 22 out of 30.

qa.q: Why does Arnab credit the thread for his better score?
qa.a: The better score came right after he started wearing it, so he feels proud and reassured, as if the thread must have caused it.

qa.q: What could Arnab compare before crediting the thread?
qa.a: He could compare with his usual scores and the whole class's, since the first test was unusually low for him and the retest was easier for everyone.

qa.q: How does Zubin explain the change in scores?
qa.a: Zubin thinks the fever during the first test and the easier retest explain it, not the thread.

grounding: Shows a teenager crediting a lucky thread for a better score when things would likely have improved anyway.

passage:
[Monsoon, family group forwards]
Harsha: ganga, mami has forwarded the same msg 6 times now
Harsha: "Neighbour's uncle drank this herbal kadha ONE night and his cough was gone next morning!! Forward to all"
Ganga: 😅 classic
Harsha: my cough's been hanging around and now everyone's pushing it on me. mami says it works because the cough went right after he drank it
Ganga: coughs often get better on their own though. he might have been getting better anyway
Ganga: and who knows what else he took, or if he saw a doctor too
Harsha: true. but it sounds so convincing when the timing fits
Ganga: timing isn't proof. drink the kadha if you like the taste, but if the cough keeps going or worries you, see the doctor
Harsha: ok. booking the college clinic tomorrow. and i'll tell mami thanks for caring 🙏

qa.q: How many times has Mami forwarded the message?
qa.a: 6 times.

qa.q: Why does the forwarded story feel convincing to Harsha?
qa.a: The cough vanished right after the kadha, and that neat timing makes the story sound true, so Harsha feels pressured and half-persuaded.

qa.q: What does Harsha decide, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: To book the college clinic, because a cough that keeps going should be checked by a doctor rather than trusted to a forwarded story.

qa.q: Why might Mami keep forwarding the message?
qa.a: Mami probably cares and wants to help, and the timing in the story makes it feel like real proof.

grounding: Shows a student receiving forwarded claims that a herbal drink cured someone right after it was taken, where the timing ignores natural recovery and other causes.

passage: Last winter my headaches came almost every evening. Manjula aunty gave me her copper bracelet. "Wear it, Leela. Mine went away in a week." I wore it, and within a week the headaches did ease off. I nearly became a believer. But I kept wondering: would the headaches have eased anyway, bracelet or not? My project deadline had also passed that week, and I had started sleeping properly again. So I tried a simple check. For the next month I wrote down each headache, the hours I slept and my screen time, and I took the bracelet off every other week. The headaches followed my sleep, not the bracelet. When they came back strongly in March, I didn't reach for charms or forwarded tips. I went to a doctor, who asked about the very things in my notebook. I gave Manjula aunty her bracelet back with a box of sweets.

qa.q: What did Leela write down for a month?
qa.a: Each headache, the hours slept and screen time.

qa.q: Why didn't Leela simply believe the bracelet worked?
qa.a: Leela felt curious and a little doubtful, noticing that the deadline had passed and sleep had improved in that same week.

qa.q: Which steps made Leela's approach wise?
qa.a: Asking what would have happened without the bracelet, tracking headaches with and without it, and seeing a doctor when the headaches came back strongly.

qa.q: How might Manjula aunty feel getting the bracelet back?
qa.a: Manjula aunty may feel a little disappointed that the bracelet didn't get the credit, but touched by the box of sweets.

grounding: Shows a person asking what would have happened without a remedy, testing it more carefully, and seeing a doctor for a real health problem.

passage: Darshan's birthday fell in the Christmas holidays, and he planned the party in his Pune flat all by himself. Pani puri, extra spicy, because everyone loved pani puri. The racing video game, because everyone loved racing. And the dinosaur film, because obviously. When his friends arrived, Rekha took one puri and fanned her mouth. Two others asked if there was cake. Nobody wanted the racing game; they wanted carrom. When he put on the dinosaur film, Rekha said, "Again? We saw it in class." Darshan stood by the TV, holding the remote, his cheeks burning. "But everyone likes this," he said quietly. Rekha shrugged, not unkindly. "You like this."

qa.q: Which film did Darshan put on?
qa.a: The dinosaur film.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel when Rekha said "Again?"
qa.a: He felt surprised and hurt, cheeks burning, because he had been sure everyone liked the same things he did.

qa.q: What could Darshan try when planning his next party?
qa.a: He could ask a few friends what they enjoy and offer a couple of choices of food and games, instead of guessing from his own favourites.

qa.q: How does Rekha see the party plan?
qa.a: Rekha sees it as Darshan's favourites rather than everyone's, which is why she says "You like this."

grounding: Shows a child assuming all his friends like the same food, game and film he does, and feeling hurt when they differ.

passage:
Monday, first week after the winter break: In the corridor, Zubin announced loudly, "Mathur sir is the worst teacher in the school. Everyone thinks so." A few people laughed. He took that as agreement.
Wednesday: In the class group chat he posted a meme about Mathur sir's slow voice. Naveen replied, "Not cool. He stayed after school for weeks to help me with calculus." Two others agreed with Naveen. Zubin stared at the screen. "Since when do you like him?"
Friday: At lunch Zubin sat stiffly. "You all ganged up on me," he told Naveen. "I just said what everyone thinks." Naveen shook his head. "You said what you think. I never agreed." Zubin looked around the table and realised he had never actually asked anyone.

qa.q: What did Zubin post in the class group chat?
qa.a: A meme about Mathur sir's slow voice.

qa.q: Why does Zubin feel attacked on Friday?
qa.a: He had assumed everyone shared his opinion, so disagreement felt like people ganging up on him rather than simply thinking differently, and he feels hurt and defensive.

qa.q: What could Zubin do before speaking for everyone next time?
qa.a: Ask others what they think, and speak for himself with "I think" instead of "everyone thinks".

qa.q: How does Naveen see Mathur sir?
qa.a: Naveen is grateful to Mathur sir for staying after school for weeks to help with calculus, so the meme felt unfair.

grounding: Shows a teenager assuming everyone shares his opinion of a teacher, speaking bluntly, then feeling attacked when others disagree.

passage: Gurleen, you came back from that wedding saying, "How can anyone in our family think that?" Sit, have some plum cake, it's Christmas. At twenty, I was the same. In college in Bangalore, all my friends read the same papers and argued only with people who already agreed. I was sure every sensible person thought as I did about the city elections. Then at Christmas lunch in Kottayam, my own uncle said the opposite, calmly, over the appam. I was so shocked I dropped my spoon. I called him old-fashioned, in front of everyone. Later my grandmother told me he had lost his shop when the new rules came in. He had reasons I had never heard, because I had never listened to anyone like him. So, Gurleen, before you call someone foolish, ask them why. That is Joseph uncle's Christmas lesson, learned the hard way.

qa.q: What did young Joseph drop when his uncle spoke?
qa.a: His spoon.

qa.q: Why was young Joseph so shocked at his uncle's view?
qa.a: Surrounded by friends who agreed with him, he was sure every sensible person thought the same, so the disagreement came as a real surprise and felt almost offensive.

qa.q: What choice at the Christmas lunch could young Joseph have made differently?
qa.a: Instead of calling his uncle old-fashioned in front of everyone, he could have asked why his uncle thought that and listened.

qa.q: Where did the uncle's view come from, according to the grandmother?
qa.a: He had lost his shop when the new rules came in, so his view came from real experience that Joseph had never heard about.

grounding: Shows a young adult who mostly met like-minded people assuming his view was nearly universal, and being shocked at a relative's differing view.

passage: Ankita, you're about to announce the new flexi-time plan assuming everyone wants it. Let me tell you what happened to your Indu didi at twenty-five, when I ran the staff welfare committee at the textile mill. I was sure everyone wanted the canteen to serve lunch later, because all my friends on the design floor ate late. Before posting the notice, something made me walk down to the loom floor and the packing unit and simply ask. The weavers wanted lunch earlier, because their shift started at six. The packers didn't care about timing at all; they wanted the canteen to stop running out of rice. I was surprised, even a bit embarrassed. So I treated the surprise as a clue and asked more questions. We ended up with two lunch slots and more rice. Ask first, Ankita. It saves a lot of notices.

qa.q: Why did the weavers want lunch earlier?
qa.a: Because their shift started at six.

qa.q: How did young Indu feel on hearing what the weavers and packers wanted?
qa.a: Indu felt surprised and a bit embarrassed, then curious, treating the surprise as a clue to learn more.

qa.q: What choice in the story made the canteen plan work?
qa.a: Walking down to the loom floor and the packing unit to ask before posting the notice, which led to two lunch slots and more rice.

qa.q: What did the packers care about most?
qa.a: The packers didn't mind the timing; they wanted the canteen to stop running out of rice.

grounding: Shows a person checking what others actually think, seeking out people unlike themselves, and treating surprise at disagreement as a sign to learn.

passage: On the morning before Tết, in their apartment in Houston, Bao was supposed to teach his little brother Mateo to fold paper lanterns for the window. Bao had made dozens. "Easy. Fold it, cut the lines, open it, glue it," he said, and his own lantern was done in a minute. Mateo stared at his crumpled sheet. "Fold it which way?" "Just fold it!" Mateo folded it the long way. "No, the other way! Why are you cutting there? I told you!" "You didn't tell me where," Mateo said, his lip wobbling. Bao threw down the scissors. "It's so obvious!" Mom looked over from the stove. "Was it obvious the first time you did it?" Bao opened his mouth, then remembered his first lantern, the one that fell apart.

qa.q: What was Bao supposed to teach Mateo?
qa.a: To fold paper lanterns for the window.

qa.q: Why does Bao get so frustrated?
qa.a: Having made dozens of lanterns, Bao can't remember not knowing how, so the steps feel obvious and Mateo's confusion makes him angry and impatient.

qa.q: What could Bao do to teach Mateo better?
qa.a: He could go slowly, show each fold and cut on his own sheet beside Mateo's, and remember his first lantern that fell apart.

qa.q: What is it like for Mateo when Bao says "It's so obvious"?
qa.a: Mateo feels lost and close to tears, because nobody told him which way to fold or where to cut.

grounding: Shows an older child teaching his younger brother, skipping steps that seem obvious to him and getting frustrated when the little one is lost.
